A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the DIQ medical data-selection study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices A–G are readable and support comparison across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, a quadrant-selection pilot, clinical-quality assessments, ablations, and transfer experiments, with detailed results in Appendix G.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds evaluated selection baselines and a validation-set-size experiment.

M1.justification: The described influence procedure changes substantially. V1 Section 3.3 aggregates learning-rate-weighted gradient products across training epochs; v2 computes Dot using a single reference checkpoint, defaulting to the pretrained model before SFT. Appendix D changes its computation reference accordingly. The quadrant priority remains unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The six medical training corpora, nine evaluation benchmarks, QA-only variants, and FineMed preference-learning coverage are retained. Huatuo-DS and MedReason disappear from the main Table 1 display but remain evaluated in Appendix G.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds actual PPL, Similarity, and LESS comparisons on Huatuo and FineMed at both 1% and 10% retention. V1's corresponding comparison included random selection and full-data training. The general-model comparisons and existing single-criterion ablations remain.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a validation-size sweep of 90, 180, 270, 360, and 450 examples for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct trained on 1% Huatuo. The default 20 validation examples per task, fine-tuning models, LoRA settings, three-epoch budget, and answer-scoring procedure otherwise remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.3 and Table 3 test sensitivity to the validation-set size used for influence estimation. This adds one focused robustness analysis; the existing single-score ablations, transfer experiments, preference-learning analysis, and clinical case study are retained.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly states that the QA-only comparison averages five runs in Section 4.2. V1's explicit five-repeat statement accompanied Table 1, without equivalent reporting for the QA experiment. This is additional run-count disclosure, not evidence of increased repetitions; neither version reports confidence intervals or variability estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial comparative results, including Huatuo 1% LESS accuracy of 40.54 versus DIQ's retained 42.78, and validation-size outcomes ranging from 42.04 at 90 examples to 43.89 at 450. Existing appendix results and distribution plots are numerically unchanged. New Section 5.2 prose also misreports the strongest ablation comparator: Figure 6 and Table 11 show Influence at 1% and Overall at 10%, not Reasoning.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the cumulative influence definition and derivation with a fixed-checkpoint Dot definition and a one-step validation-loss relationship. It adds an explicit Taylor remainder, small-learning-rate and bounded-curvature conditions, and a preconditioner ordering claim. However, Appendix D does not contain the promised full derivation or optimizer extensions.

C1.justification: The joint difficulty–influence selection, clinical-quality, and 1–10% data-efficiency claims remain. V2 modestly broadens the abstract and introduction's outperformance claim from the baseline to competing baseline methods, supported by its newly evaluated selectors, and specifies Dot in the conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies cross-family transfer as budget-sensitive and explicitly discusses negative cases, refining v1's broader robustness language. It interprets the new validation-size results as a quality–compute tradeoff and adds more specific clinical and QA-selection explanations. The limitation concerning models of at least 70B parameters remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds a 4096-dimensional gradient-projection specification and baseline computation details. However, it removes v1's code/data availability link and the difficulty classifier's GPT-4.1 annotation information, 20,000-question corpus description, source list, and 18,000/2,000 training/test split; these are not recovered in Appendix C. The fine-tuning hyperparameters, hardware, and evaluation prompts remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Sentence-BERT and Meta-Rater for the new selection baselines, plus GPT-4 and Gemini technical reports. Previously cited LESS and TracIn now support explicit comparator descriptions. The broader positioning around data-efficient medical fine-tuning remains similar.

P1.justification: The method exposition, related-work prose, main-results discussion, analysis, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Subsections are renamed, training and evaluation descriptions are combined, and baseline and validation-size subsections are introduced. Author/header information and citation style also change; most appendix prose is retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially reorganized into retention groups with additional comparator rows, shading, and best/second-best highlighting; a new validation-size table is added. Figure 2's labels and caption are revised. Document typography and page composition change throughout, including substantial redistribution of appendix plots and prompt boxes, while the original 17 figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The added nonrandom baselines and validation-size analysis address real weaknesses in v1's empirical evaluation, and the transfer discussion becomes more qualified. These gains coexist with lost classifier-training and code-access information, missing derivations promised by Section 3.3, and new erroneous ablation summaries: the 1% margin over the strongest comparator is 0.11, not the stated 0.89. The empirical benefits and regressions in reproducibility and internal consistency do not establish a reliable net direction.
